verses.text: Now concerning the things about which you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman.
But, because of sexual immoralities, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband.
Let the husband give his wife the affection owed her,  and likewise also the wife her husband.
The wife doesn’t have authority over her own body, but the husband. Likewise also the husband doesn’t have authority over his own body, but the wife.

Don’t deprive one another, unless it is by consent for a season, that you may give yourselves to fasting and prayer, and may be together again, that Satan doesn’t tempt you because of your lack of self-control.
But this I say by way of concession, not of commandment.
Yet I wish that all men were like me. However each man has his own gift from God, one of this kind, and another of that kind.
But I say to the unmarried and to widows, it is good for them if they remain even as I am.
But if they don’t have self-control, let them marry. For it’s better to marry than to burn.
But to the married I command — not I, but the Lord — that the wife not leave her husband
(but if she departs, let her remain unmarried, or else be reconciled to her husband), and that the husband not leave his wife.
But to the rest I — not the Lord — say, if any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she is content to live with him, let him not leave her.
The woman who has an unbelieving husband, and he is content to live with her, let her not leave her husband.
For the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified in the husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy.
Yet if the unbeliever departs, let there be separation. The brother or the sister is not under bondage in such cases, but God has called us in peace.
For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?
Only, as the Lord has distributed to each man, as God has called each, so let him walk. So I command in all the assemblies.
Was anyone called having been circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised. Has anyone been called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised.
Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God.
Let each man stay in that calling in which he was called.
Were you called being a bondservant? Don’t let that bother you, but if you get an opportunity to become free, use it.
For he who was called in the Lord being a bondservant is the Lord’s free man. Likewise he who was called being free is Christ’s bondservant.
You were bought with a price. Don’t become bondservants of men.
Brothers, let each man, in whatever condition he was called, stay in that condition with God.
Now concerning virgins, I have no commandment from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be trustworthy.
I think that it is good therefore, because of the distress that is on us, that it is good for a man to be as he is.
Are you bound to a wife? Don’t seek to be freed. Are you free from a wife? Don’t seek a wife.
But if you marry, you have not sinned. If a virgin marries, she has not sinned. Yet such will have oppression in the flesh, and I want to spare you.
But I say this, brothers: the time is short, that from now on, both those who have wives may be as though they had none;
and those who weep, as though they didn’t weep; and those who rejoice, as though they didn’t rejoice; and those who buy, as though they didn’t possess;
and those who use the world, as not using it to the fullest. For the mode of this world passes away.
But I desire to have you to be free from cares. He who is unmarried is concerned for the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord;
but he who is married is concerned about the things of the world, how he may please his wife.

There is also a difference between a wife and a virgin. The unmarried woman cares about the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and in spirit. But she who is married cares about the things of the world — how she may please her husband.
This I say for your own profit; not that I may ensnare you, but for that which is appropriate, and that you may attend to the Lord without distraction.
But if any man thinks that he is behaving inappropriately toward his virgin, if she is past the flower of her age, and if need so requires, let him do what he desires. He doesn’t sin. Let them marry.
But he who stands steadfast in his heart, having no urgency, but has power over his own will, and has determined in his own heart to keep his own virgin, does well.
So then both he who gives his own virgin in marriage does well, and he who doesn’t give her in marriage does better.
A wife is bound by law for as long as her husband lives; but if the husband is dead, she is free to be married to whomever she desires, only in the Lord.
But she is happier if she stays as she is, in my judgment, and I think that I also have God’s Spirit.

footnotes.content: Paul answers a hard question the Corinthians asked him in writing. He opens with a truth: there's real goodness in singleness, in undivided devotion to the Lord. Not everyone is called to it, but where the Lord gives that gift, it's a gift.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet marriage isn't sin—it's a remedy and a good design. Paul isn't setting up a hierarchy; he's naming reality: most of us need that companionship, that faithfulness. Better to marry than to burn with unfulfilled desire.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here's tenderness in the middle of a doctrinal chapter: husbands and wives owe each other affection. Not duty alone—genuine care and nearness. Jesus didn't come to make marriage transactional; He sanctifies the whole thing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A stunning turn: in marriage, neither spouse owns their own body—they belong to each other, fully. It's mutual surrendering, not dominion. The Lord teaches us that real freedom comes through covenant, not independence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even seasons of fasting and prayer need consent—nothing coerced. And when they return to each other, the closeness stands as a hedge against temptation. The Lord knows us: we need both pursuit of Him and the anchor of covenant companionship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul's careful here: this is wise counsel, not divine command. He knows believers need room to breathe, to hear the Lord themselves. Humility in leadership means not claiming more authority than you have.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He wishes all had his gift—singleness before the Lord. But he knows: gifts differ. The Spirit distributes them, not culture, not circumstance. My calling isn't your calling, and that's the way God made it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To the unmarried and widows, Paul names the goodness of staying as they are—a mirror to his own life. But notice: no shame in marrying either. Both paths honor the Lord when walked with Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A clear-eyed realism: if someone hasn't the grace to remain single, let them marry. It's not failure—it's wisdom. The Lord is far more concerned with our faithfulness where He's placed us than with our adherence to a standard He hasn't given us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here Paul marks a distinction: this comes from the Lord Himself. Husbands mustn't leave their wives. In Matthew 5, Jesus taught it plainly—the permanence of covenant is His design, not Paul's opinion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even when a marriage fractures, the door to reconciliation stays open—and it should. Remaining unmarried while separated, or seeking restoration: these honor the covenant that Christ will never break with His own people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Paul speaks where Christ hasn't given explicit instruction: a believer married to an unbeliever. His wisdom: don't flee. If your spouse is willing to stay, there's grace to stay together. The Lord can work even in that tension.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The same applies to believing women with unbelieving husbands. Paul's guidance is symmetric: the wife, like the husband, shouldn't initiate separation. Love doesn't flee; it stays and loves the one God gave.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A mysterious grace: the believing spouse—by their faith, their prayers, their presence—somehow sanctifies the unbelieving one and the children. It's not saving power, but a real covering. The Lord honors the faithfulness of one who loves despite the divide.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But if the unbeliever chooses to leave, the believer isn't bound. You can't hold someone who won't stay, and the Lord doesn't require the impossible. He has called us to live in peace, not in a prison of your own making.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A tender question: how do you know if your faithfulness might save your spouse? You don't. But the Lord does—and He calls us to love without knowing the outcome. That's what trust looks like when marriage is hard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul pivots to a bigger principle: walk in the calling God has given you. Whether single or married, circumcised or not—the Lord distributes His gifts. Obedience isn't about changing your status; it's about faithfulness where you stand. This becomes his refrain to all the churches.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A man called while circumcised shouldn't try to hide it; one called uncircumcised shouldn't get circumcised to fit in. Your past, your body, your origin—the Lord meets you there. No need to rewrite your story.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: None of the cultural markers matter in the end—neither circumcision nor its absence. What matters is the keeping of God's commandments: love, faithfulness, obedience to the Lord. Everything else is dust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Stay in your calling. Not because you'll never have opportunity to change, but because the Lord often works deepest where you are already planted. Trust that your place isn't an accident.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even a slave called by the Lord has dignity. But if freedom comes—and Paul opens the door—use it. The Lord doesn't require you to remain in bondage when escape is available. He honors both faithfulness in hard places and the pursuit of freedom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A radical reframing: the slave in the Lord becomes His freedman—truly free inside where it matters most. And the free man becomes Christ's servant—bound by love to the One who bought him. In Him, all earthly status dissolves into real liberty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You were bought with a price—Christ's own blood. So don't trade your freedom by becoming enslaved to human opinion, status, or expectation. You belong to Him now, and that settles everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Whether married or single, free or enslaved, your one calling is to be with God where you are. Not restless, not comparing your lot to someone else's—just present with the Lord in your actual condition. That's where grace meets us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul moves to virgins—young believers deciding their path. He has no direct command from the Lord on this, so he offers his judgment humbly: he's been met with mercy, so his counsel comes from a heart that knows grace. He doesn't claim what he doesn't have.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Corinthians faced real distress—perhaps persecution, maybe famine. In that moment, Paul sees singleness as practical mercy: fewer entanglements, fewer mouths to feed, clearer heart for the Lord. But it's situational wisdom, not universal law.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bound to a wife? Don't seek divorce. Single? Don't chase marriage just to escape loneliness. Stay put. The grass looks greener from here, but the Lord wants you still and faithful in your actual plot.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But—and Paul softens—if you marry, you haven't sinned. There's no shame in it. He just wants to spare you hardship: marriage in a fractured world brings real trouble. But trouble doesn't disqualify love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The time is short—an old cry from Paul's heart, echoed in Scripture. Because the end draws near, even married believers should hold their marriages loosely, focused on what lasts. Not that the marriage doesn't matter; it does. But it's not your ultimate.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Weep as if you don't weep, rejoice as if you don't rejoice—a paradox of detachment in the middle of attachment. You feel it all, but not as your final word. The Lord alone is your stability when everything else shifts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The mode of this world passes away—the structures, the urgencies, the fashions. So use the world—yes, buy, work, live—but not as if it's permanent. There's a lightness the Lord calls us to, a refusal to nail our hope to what will turn to dust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul wants freedom from cares for them—not cruel indifference, but a kind of unconcern that lets them seek the Lord. The unmarried person can ask: how do I please the Lord? That's the one thought worth being consumed by.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The married one's mind splits: pleasing the Lord and pleasing the spouse. It's not sin; it's just divided attention. A real cost, real complexity—which is why Paul doesn't shame the single, but neither does he shame those who take on that weight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The same applies to women: unmarried, a virgin can be holy in body and spirit, undistracted in her pursuit of the Lord. Married, she's pulled toward pleasing her husband. Paul names the difference plainly—not to shame, but to illuminate choice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He says this for their profit, not to trap them. His heart is that they attend to the Lord without distraction—to be fully present where they are, whether alone or together. That's the mercy behind the counsel.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A father concerned about his unmarried daughter reaching maturity—if he feels called to let her marry, no sin lies there. Paul honors both the call to singleness and the father's care to provide for her future. Love looks different in different seasons.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But if a father stands firm in his heart, resolved to keep his daughter single and devoted to the Lord—no pressure, no urgency—he does well. It's a matter of the will, not duty, and the Lord honors the voluntary offering.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Both paths do well: giving your daughter in marriage, or keeping her devoted to the Lord. But Paul tilts slightly toward the single life—more freedom to serve, fewer earthly entanglements. Yet it's a gentle tilt, not a command.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A widow is bound only as long as her husband lives. Once he's gone, she's free to marry whom she will—but only in the Lord. That phrase captures everything: choose someone who walks with Jesus. It's the one non-negotiable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in Paul's closing: a widow who stays unmarried finds deeper rest. We live in a culture that says remarriage after loss is mandatory joy, yet Paul quietly affirms that some find their whole joy in the Lord alone. His Spirit is with him in that counsel, and it stands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
